justice: Spatial allocation favors the carriageway: the asphalt road is continuous and wide enough for vehicles, while there is no clearly defined sidewalk on either side.
Accessibility is limited because the street edge near the tiled building and the tree-lined wall lacks curb ramps, tactile paving, or any marked pedestrian zone.
Fairness across user groups is weakened by roadside obstructions, including the row of red waste bins and utility poles, which reduce usable edge space for non-motorized users.
safety: The lane appears low-speed and lightly trafficked, which lowers collision risk compared with a major road.
Safety is reduced by the absence of marked pedestrian crossings, sidewalks, or protective separation between people walking and vehicles.
Overhead utility wires and poles, along with a narrow roadway leading into a bend or enclosed segment, may reduce perceived and actual visibility and clearance.
livability: The dense green trees on the right provide some environmental quality and soften the street scene.
The area appears quiet and low-intensity, but there are no visible active frontages, shops, seating, or public amenities that support daily social life.
The blank and partially boarded facade of the building on the left, combined with the utilitarian waste bins on the right, makes the street feel more service-oriented than socially vibrant.
sustainability: Street trees on the right contribute to shade, cooling, and small-scale ecological value.
There is no visible bike lane, bus stop, transit facility, or dedicated pedestrian infrastructure to support low-carbon travel choices.
The scene is dominated by hard asphalt and building surfaces, with no obvious permeable paving, bioswale, rain garden, or other stormwater infrastructure.
aesthetics: The mature green tree canopy and clear blue sky create a pleasant natural backdrop.
Visual quality is weakened by exposed overhead wires, utility poles, and the row of bright red waste bins at the street edge.
The building on the left has a worn appearance, including bricked-up openings and patchy wall surfaces, which reduces overall visual coherence.
comfort: Thermal comfort is mixed: the trees on the right provide shade, but the left side and the open asphalt surface are highly exposed to sun.
Physical comfort is limited because there is no visible bench, resting area, or dedicated pedestrian path separated from the roadway.
Psychological comfort is moderate at best: the street seems quiet, but the narrow shared-space condition and lack of clear walking space can make users feel uncertain.
walkability: Walkability is low because there is no continuous sidewalk or clearly marked pedestrian route along the road.
Objects at the edge of the street, especially the red trash bins and utility poles, can constrain walking space and force pedestrians into the carriageway.
Although the street appears calm and shaded in parts by trees, the absence of crossings, curb design, and pedestrian-oriented amenities limits walking appeal.
bikeability: Bikeability is poor because there is no dedicated bike lane, shoulder, or pavement marking for cyclists.
Cyclists would need to share a narrow roadway with any motor vehicles, with no physical protection or intersection guidance.
The quiet local-road character is somewhat helpful, but roadside obstacles and the lack of bicycle parking or cycling facilities keep the score low.
